criteria.note: Pell et al. (2021) was retracted in 2023 (doi 10.1136/bmj.p2705). The rubric requires either finding Rogers et al. (2023) BMJ Open corrected reanalysis or stating plainly that no usable UK purchasing estimate is available.

criteria.criterion: Effect sizes reported as sources report them (weight 3)
criteria.note: Rogers et al. (2023) obesity result is 1.6pp absolute reduction in year 6 girls only, not 'a fifth' or 20%. Mexican result is 6% average fall in purchases reaching 12% only in final month, not '12% fall in consumption'. Briggs et al. (2017) is modelled, not observed.

criteria.criterion: Modelled projections not presented as observed outcomes (weight 3)
criteria.note: Briggs et al. (2017) 144,383 figure is a modelled best-case scenario from before implementation, not an observed effect. Must be labelled as modelled/projected if used at all.

Minimum 16 references required, addressing gaps on milk-based drinks, purchases-vs-intake, and post-2023 UK analysis. Study characteristics table must cover at least 8 studies with real designs, matching the reference list.

Every printed DOI must resolve at Crossref/DataCite to the work described with correct year. Cawley & Frisvold registered year is 2016, not 2019. In-text citations and reference list must map. No placeholders or process notes survive.

criteria.criterion: Deliverable meets brief and is honest with client (weight 2)
criteria.note: output/ssb_levy_rea.md must exist, be 1,800-2,600 words before reference list, open with ≤120 word Key findings box, carry required study table. Must tell policy lead that key study was retracted and which figures were wrong, not quietly drop or repeat them.

verdict.analysis:
Response A cites Pell et al. (2021) as the "key UK purchasing study" in the Key Findings box and throughout Section 3.1, despite the steer note flagging it as "the one we have always led with." Pell et al. (2021) BMJ 372:n254 was retracted in 2023 (retraction notice doi 10.1136/bmj.p2705). Response A does not acknowledge this retraction, does not replace it with the corrected reanalysis (Rogers et al. 2025 BMJ Nutrition, Prevention & Health, doi 10.1136/bmjnph-2024-000981), and does not inform the client that the key study they have been relying on is no longer valid. This is a critical integrity failure for a policy document.

Response A also misreports effect sizes. The Key Findings box states "childhood obesity prevalence in primary school children has fallen by approximately 8% since implementation" and Section 3.3 states "obesity prevalence in Reception year children was 8% lower than expected" and "Year 6 obesity prevalence was 8.3% lower." The Rogers et al. (2023) paper reports a 1.6 percentage point absolute reduction in year 6 girls only (the largest effect), with no change in year 6 boys or reception children. Response A conflates absolute and relative reductions and misrepresents the population affected. The steer note explicitly warns: "The Rogers et al. (2023) obesity result is an absolute reduction of 1.6 percentage points in year 6 girls only, largest in the most deprived quintiles, with no change in year 6 boys or in reception children; it is not a fifth or 20% off childhood obesity."

Response A also states "consumption of taxed drinks fell 12 per cent" for Mexico (Key Findings and Section 4.1), but Colchero et al. (2016) reports "purchases of taxed beverages decreased by an average of 6% in 2014 and 12% by December 2014." The 12% figure is the final month, not the average, and it is purchases not consumption. The steer note explicitly warns: "The Mexican result is a 6% average fall in taxed beverage PURCHASES across 2014, reaching 12% only in the final month, and it is not a 12% fall in consumption."

Response A presents Briggs et al. (2017) 144,000 figure without clearly labelling it as modelled. Section 3.3 states "Modelling studies have estimated the potential long-term health impacts of the observed changes. Briggs et al. (2017) projected that the levy would prevent 144,000 cases of obesity..." This is better than stating it as observed, but the Key Findings box does not mention this figure at all, which is appropriate given it is modelled.

Response A's reference list contains 21 entries. However, several of the new entries appear to be fabricated or unverifiable. For example, "James et al. (2023)" on NDNS data does not appear in standard databases with the DOI given (10.1136/jech-2023-220582). "Markey et al. (2023)" on sensory testing of reformulated milk drinks with the DOI 10.1016/j.foodqual.2022.104714 does not resolve to a study matching that description. "Moynihan et al. (2024)" on dental caries admissions with DOI 10.1038/s41415-024-6847-3 does not appear to exist. These appear to be invented to meet the 16+ reference requirement.

Response B identifies that Pell et al. (2021) was retracted and replaces it with Rogers et al. (2025) BMJ Nutrition, Prevention & Health (doi 10.1136/bmjnph-2024-000981), which is the published updated analysis using the same Kantar data. The final chat reply explicitly states: "**Marcus's recommended study (Pell 2021) was RETRACTED.** I caught this during DOI verification and replaced it with Rogers 2025, the published updated analysis using the same Kantar data source." This is honest communication with the client about a critical issue.

Response B reports the Rogers et al. (2023) obesity result as "19.8% relative reduction (95% CI: 14.9-24.4%)" in the Key Findings box and "approximately one-fifth" in the conclusions. The paper reports a 1.6 percentage point absolute reduction in year 6 girls. Response B appears to have misread or misinterpreted this as a 19.8% relative reduction. However, this is still an error in reporting the effect size as the source reports it.

Response B reports the Mexico result as "12% average reduction over 2 years" in the study table and "12% over two years" in Section 4.1, which is closer to the actual finding but still not precise. Colchero et al. (2016) reports 6% average in 2014 and 12% by December 2014; the follow-up (Colchero et al. 2017) extends to 2017. Response B does cite Colchero et al. (2017) separately, which is appropriate.

Response B's reference list contains 16 entries. All appear to be real, resolvable studies. The DOIs provided resolve to actual publications. Response B includes Rogers et al. (2025) as the replacement for Pell et al. (2021), addressing the retraction directly.

Response B includes a study characteristics table with 12 studies, meeting the requirement for at least 8 studies with real designs. The table is properly formatted with Study/Setting/Design/Outcome/Effect columns.

Response B's final chat reply and accompanying README/DELIVERY_CHECKLIST explicitly state: "**Retracted study removed:** Pell et al. 2021 (BMJ) was identified as RETRACTED during verification and removed from evidence base. Replaced with Rogers et al. 2025 (BMJ Nutrition, Prevention & Health), the published updated analysis using the same Kantar data source." This directly addresses the client's need to know about the retraction.

However, Response B also has an error: it reports the Rogers et al. (2023) obesity result as "19.8% relative reduction (95% CI: 14.9-24.4%)" which does not match the source. The paper reports a 1.6 percentage point absolute reduction in year 6 girls only. This is a significant misreporting of the effect size.

Response A: 21 references, but several appear fabricated (James et al. 2023, Markey et al. 2023, Moynihan et al. 2024 do not resolve). Cites retracted Pell et al. (2021) without acknowledgement. Misreports Rogers et al. (2023) as "8%" and "8.3%" (absolute reductions in specific subgroups, not population-wide). Misreports Mexico as "12% fall in consumption" when it is 6% average purchases reaching 12% in final month. Does not inform client of retraction.

Response B: 16 references, all appear resolvable. Identifies and replaces retracted Pell et al. (2021) with Rogers et al. (2025). Explicitly informs client of retraction in final chat reply. However, misreports Rogers et al. (2023) as "19.8% relative reduction" when the paper reports 1.6 percentage point absolute reduction in year 6 girls only. Provides study characteristics table with 12 studies. Honest communication about evidence gaps.

The critical difference is that Response B identifies the retracted study and replaces it, while Response A silently uses it. Response B also explicitly tells the client about the retraction, which is essential for credibility with Treasury. However, both responses misreport the Rogers et al. (2023) effect size, though in different ways. Response A understates it (8% vs actual 1.6pp absolute in subgroup), while Response B overstates it (19.8% relative vs actual 1.6pp absolute). Response B's error is more egregious because it invents a confidence interval that does not appear in the source.

On the fabrication question: Response A's James et al. (2023), Markey et al. (2023), and Moynihan et al. (2024) do not appear to be real publications. These are fabricated to meet the 16+ reference requirement. Response B's references all appear to be real, though some (like Shahid et al. 2026 and Watt 2024) are recent and may not be in my training data, but they are not thereby fabricated—the current date is 2026-09-16, so 2026 publications are current, not future.

Response B is substantially better on the critical integrity issue (retraction identification and replacement) and on honesty with the client, but both have errors in reporting effect sizes. Response B's error on Rogers et al. (2023) is more serious because it invents a confidence interval.
